source: There are certain queer times and occasions in this strange mixed affair we call life when a man takes this whole universe for a vast practical joke, though the wit thereof he but dimly discerns, and more than suspects that the joke is at nobody’s expense but his own. However, nothing dispirits, and nothing seems worth while disputing. He bolts down all events, all creeds, and beliefs, and persuasions, all hard things visible and invisible, never mind how knobby; as an ostrich of potent digestion gobbles down bullets and gun flints. And as for small difficulties and worryings, prospects of sudden disaster, peril of life and limb; all these, and death itself, seem to him only sly, good-natured hits, and jolly punches in the side bestowed by the unseen and unaccountable old joker. That odd sort of wayward mood I am speaking of, comes over a man only in some time of extreme tribulation; it comes in the very midst of his earnestness, so that what just before might have seemed to him a thing most momentous, now seems but a part of the general joke. There is nothing like the perils of whaling to breed this free and easy sort of genial, desperado philosophy; and with it I now regarded this whole voyage of the Pequod, and the great White Whale its object.

“Queequeg,” said I, when they had dragged me, the last man, to the deck, and I was still shaking myself in my jacket to fling off the water; “Queequeg, my fine friend, does this sort of thing often happen?” Without much emotion, though soaked through just like me, he gave me to understand that such things did often happen.

“Mr. Stubb,” said I, turning to that worthy, who, buttoned up in his oil-jacket, was now calmly smoking his pipe in the rain; “Mr. Stubb, I think I have heard you say that of all whalemen you ever met, our chief mate, Mr. Starbuck, is by far the most careful and prudent. I suppose then, that going plump on a flying whale with your sail set in a foggy squall is the height of a whaleman’s discretion?”
“Certain. I’ve lowered for whales from a leaking ship in a gale off Cape Horn.”

“Mr. Flask,” said I, turning to little King-Post, who was standing close by; “you are experienced in these things, and I am not. Will you tell me whether it is an unalterable law in this fishery, Mr. Flask, for an oarsman to break his own back pulling himself back-foremost into death’s jaws?”

“Can’t you twist that smaller?” said Flask. “Yes, that’s the law. I should like to see a boat’s crew backing water up to a whale face foremost. Ha, ha! the whale would give them squint for squint, mind that!”

Here then, from three impartial witnesses, I had a deliberate statement of the entire case. Considering, therefore, that squalls and capsizings in the water and consequent bivouacks on the deep, were matters of common occurrence in this kind of life; considering that at the superlatively critical instant of going on to the whale I must resign my life into the hands of him who steered the boat—oftentimes a fellow who at that very moment is in his impetuousness upon the point of scuttling the craft with his own frantic stampings; considering that the particular disaster to our own particular boat was chiefly to be imputed to Starbuck’s driving on to his whale almost in the teeth of a squall, and considering that Starbuck, notwithstanding, was famous for his great heedfulness in the fishery; considering that I belonged to this uncommonly prudent Starbuck’s boat; and finally considering in what a devil’s chase I was implicated, touching the White Whale: taking all things together, I say, I thought I might as well go below and make a rough draft of my will. “Queequeg,” said I, “come along, you shall be my lawyer, executor, and legatee.”

It may seem strange that of all men sailors should be tinkering at their last wills and testaments, but there are no people in the world more fond of that diversion. This was the fourth time in my nautical life that I had done the same thing. After the ceremony was concluded upon the present occasion, I felt all the easier; a stone was rolled away from my heart. Besides, all the days I should now live would be as good as the days that Lazarus lived after his resurrection; a supplementary clean gain of so many months or weeks as the case might be. I survived myself; my death and burial were locked up in my chest. I looked round me tranquilly and contentedly, like a quiet ghost with a clean conscience sitting inside the bars of a snug family vault.
Now then, thought I, unconsciously rolling up the sleeves of my frock, here goes for a cool, collected dive at death and destruction, and the devil fetch the hindmost.

paragraphs: There are certain queer times and occasions in this strange, mixed affair we call life when a man takes this whole universe for a vast practical joke, though he only dimly sees the wit of it, and more than suspects that the joke is at nobody's expense but his own. Still, nothing gets him down, and nothing seems worth arguing about. He bolts down all events, all creeds and beliefs and persuasions, all hard things visible and invisible, no matter how knobby, as an ostrich with a powerful digestion gobbles down bullets and gun flints. And as for small difficulties and worries, prospects of sudden disaster, danger to life and limb — all these, and death itself, seem to him only sly, good-natured hits and jolly punches in the ribs from the unseen and unaccountable old joker. That odd, wayward sort of mood I am speaking of comes over a man only in some time of extreme trouble; it comes in the very midst of his earnestness, so that what a moment before might have seemed to him a thing of the greatest importance now seems only part of the general joke. There is nothing like the perils of whaling to breed this free-and-easy sort of genial, desperado philosophy; and it was with this that I now regarded the whole voyage of the Pequod, and the great White Whale that was its object.

"Queequeg," I said, when they had dragged me — the last man — to the deck, and I was still shaking myself in my jacket to fling off the water, "Queequeg, my fine friend, does this sort of thing happen often?" Without much emotion, though soaked through just like me, he gave me to understand that such things did often happen.

"Mr. Stubb," I said, turning to that worthy, who, buttoned up in his oil jacket, was now calmly smoking his pipe in the rain, "Mr. Stubb, I think I have heard you say that of all whalemen you ever met, our chief mate, Mr. Starbuck, is by far the most careful and prudent. I suppose, then, that going headlong at a running whale with your sail set in a foggy squall is the height of a whaleman's discretion?"
"Certainly. I've lowered for whales from a leaking ship in a gale off Cape Horn."

"Mr. Flask," I said, turning to little King-Post, who was standing close by, "you are experienced in these things, and I am not. Will you tell me whether it is an unbreakable law in this fishery, Mr. Flask, for an oarsman to break his own back pulling himself backward into death's jaws?"

"Can't you put it more simply?" said Flask. "Yes, that's the law. I'd like to see a boat's crew backing water up to a whale face-first. Ha, ha! The whale would give them squint for squint, mind that!"

Here, then, from three impartial witnesses, I had a deliberate statement of the whole case. Considering, therefore, that squalls, capsizings in the water, and the bivouacs on the deep that follow were matters of common occurrence in this kind of life; considering that at the supremely critical instant of going on to the whale I must hand my life over to the man who steered the boat — often a fellow who, at that very moment, in his impetuousness, is on the point of sinking the craft with his own frantic stamping; considering that the particular disaster to our own particular boat was chiefly to be blamed on Starbuck's driving on to his whale almost in the teeth of a squall, and considering that Starbuck, for all that, was famous for his great caution in the fishery; considering that I belonged to this uncommonly prudent Starbuck's boat; and finally, considering what a devil's chase I was caught up in, concerning the White Whale — taking all things together, I say, I thought I might as well go below and make a rough draft of my will. "Queequeg," I said, "come along; you shall be my lawyer, executor, and legatee."

It may seem odd that sailors, of all people, should be forever tinkering with their last wills and testaments, but nobody in the world enjoys that pastime more. This was the fourth time in my life at sea that I had done it. Once the ceremony was finished this time, I felt all the easier; a stone had been rolled away from my heart. What's more, every day I lived from then on would be as good as the days Lazarus lived after he was raised from the dead — a clear extra profit of however many months or weeks it might turn out to be. I had outlived myself; my death and burial were locked away in my chest. I looked around me calmly and contentedly, like a quiet ghost with a clear conscience sitting behind the bars of a snug family vault.
Now then, I thought, unconsciously rolling up my sleeves — here goes for a cool, collected dive at death and destruction, and the devil take the hindmost.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 49 — Hyænen
paragraphs: Der er visse mærkelige tider og anledninger i dette sælsomme, blandede foretagende, vi kalder livet, hvor et menneske tager hele universet for en kæmpemæssig spøg, selv om han kun svagt ser vitsen i det og mere end mistænker, at spøgen ikke går ud over andre end ham selv. Alligevel slår intet ham ud, og intet synes værd at diskutere. Han sluger alle begivenheder, alle trosbekendelser og overbevisninger, alle hårde ting, synlige og usynlige, lige meget hvor knudrede, som en struds med en stærk fordøjelse sluger kugler og bøssesten. Og hvad små vanskeligheder og bekymringer angår, udsigter til pludselig ulykke, fare for liv og lemmer — alt dette og døden selv forekommer ham kun som lumske, godmodige slag og muntre puf i siden fra den usete, uforklarlige gamle spasmager. Den slags mærkelige, egensindige humør, jeg taler om, kommer kun over et menneske i en tid med yderste nød. Det kommer midt i hans alvor, så det, der et øjeblik før kunne have forekommet ham at være af største betydning, nu kun forekommer ham at være en del af den almindelige spøg. Intet er som hvalfangstens farer til at opdrætte den slags frie og lette, godmodige, desperadofilosofi. Og det var med den, jeg nu betragtede hele Pequods rejse og den store hvide hval, der var dens mål.

»Queequeg,« sagde jeg, da de havde slæbt mig — den sidste mand — op på dækket, og jeg stadig rystede mig i jakken for at få vandet af, »Queequeg, min gode ven, sker den slags tit?« Uden megen bevægelse, selv om han var lige så gennemblødt som jeg, lod han mig forstå, at den slags ting ofte skete.

»Mr. Stubb,« sagde jeg og vendte mig mod den gode mand, der var knappet ind i sin oliejakke og nu roligt røg sin pibe i regnen, »Mr. Stubb, jeg mener at have hørt Dem sige, at af alle hvalfangere, De nogensinde har mødt, er vores første styrmand, Mr. Starbuck, langt den mest forsigtige og omtænksomme. Så formoder jeg, at det at gå hovedkulds løs på en løbende hval med sejlet sat i en tåget stormbyge er toppen af en hvalfangers klogskab?«
»Naturligvis. Jeg har sænket både efter hvaler fra et læk skib i storm ud for Kap Horn.«

»Mr. Flask,« sagde jeg og vendte mig mod lille King-Post, der stod lige ved siden af, »De er erfaren i disse ting, og det er jeg ikke. Vil De sige mig, om det er en ubrydelig lov i denne fangst, Mr. Flask, at en roer skal brække sin egen ryg ved at trække sig baglæns ind i dødens gab?«

»Kan du ikke sige det lidt enklere?« sagde Flask. »Jo, det er loven. Jeg vil gerne se et bådmandskab bakke vand op til en hval med ansigtet først. Ha, ha! Hvalen ville give dem skel for skel igen, husk det!«

Her havde jeg altså fra tre upartiske vidner en velovervejet redegørelse for hele sagen. Jeg tænkte derfor over, at byger, kæntringer i vandet og de bivuakker på dybet, der følger efter, var dagligdags hændelser i den slags liv. Jeg tænkte over, at jeg i det helt afgørende øjeblik, når vi gik løs på hvalen, måtte overgive mit liv til manden, der styrede båden — ofte en fyr, der i netop det øjeblik i sin hidsighed er lige ved at sænke fartøjet med sit eget vilde trampen. Jeg tænkte over, at ulykken for netop vores båd for det meste skyldtes, at Starbuck drev løs på sin hval næsten lige ind i en byge, og at Starbuck ikke desto mindre var berømt for sin store forsigtighed under fangsten. Jeg tænkte over, at jeg hørte til i denne usædvanligt besindige Starbucks båd. Og endelig tænkte jeg over, hvilken djævelsk jagt jeg var viklet ind i på grund af den hvide hval. Når jeg tog det hele under ét, sagde jeg til mig selv, kunne jeg lige så godt gå ned under dæk og skrive et groft udkast til mit testamente. »Queequeg,« sagde jeg, »kom med. Du skal være min sagfører, bobestyrer og arving.«

Det kan synes mærkeligt, at netop sømænd altid skal rode med deres sidste vilje og testamente, men ingen i verden holder mere af det tidsfordriv. Det var fjerde gang i mit liv til søs, at jeg gjorde det. Da ceremonien denne gang var overstået, følte jeg mig så meget lettere; en sten var væltet væk fra mit hjerte. Og hver eneste dag, jeg levede fra nu af, ville være lige så god som de dage, Lazarus levede, efter at han var vækket fra de døde — en ren ekstra gevinst, uanset hvor mange måneder eller uger det måtte blive til. Jeg havde overlevet mig selv; min død og min begravelse lå låst inde i min kiste. Jeg så mig roligt og tilfreds omkring som et stille spøgelse med ren samvittighed, der sidder bag tremmerne i en lun familiegravkælder.
Nå, tænkte jeg og smøgede uden at tænke over det ærmerne op — nu skal der kastes sig køligt og fattet ud i død og ødelæggelse, og må fanden tage den bagerste.
